rationale: The book offers a significantly more robust scriptural derivation for 'the heart of the earth' than the traditional consensus. By cross-referencing Ezekiel 5:5 and 38:12, the book demonstrates that Scripture already identifies Jerusalem as the 'midst' or 'navel' of the earth/land. This establishes a structural parallel with Jonah being cast into the 'heart of the seas' (Jonah 2:3), creating a precise land/sea (Israel/Gentile) dichotomy. Furthermore, applying this geographic referent resolves the notorious 'three days and three nights' chronological problem by encompassing Jesus' time in the custody of Jerusalem (starting at the Thursday night arrest). The traditional 'tomb' interpretation relies on an unsupported spatial metaphor—no scripture refers to the grave as the 'heart of the earth'—and continually struggles to fit three days and nights into the Friday-to-Sunday entombment. The book’s macro-typology, mapping the entire Jonah narrative scene-by-scene to the Passion, provides overwhelming explanatory power that the isolated traditional reading lacks.
book_core_identification: Jerusalem — the navel and heart of the land.
book_secondary_elaborations: The three days and three nights begin with Jesus' arrest and custody under the city's power, not solely His entombment.
The 'heart of the earth' perfectly mirrors Jonah's descent into the 'heart of the seas' (the gentile world).
The 'great fish' represents the Roman ruler/empire to which Jerusalem (the ship) surrendered Him.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The phrase 'heart of the earth' refers to the physical tomb or the subterranean realm of the dead (Sheol/Hades), functioning as a direct spatial parallel to the 'belly of the great fish' where Jonah was confined.
material_core_denial: The counter-interpretation insists the phrase is a spatial metaphor for burial or the afterlife, completely denying that it acts as a geographic identifier for the city of Jerusalem.
counter_case: Jonah explicitly calls his location the 'belly of hell' (Sheol) in Jonah 2:2, heavily implying a correlation to the realm of the dead.
The anatomical metaphor of 'heart' corresponds cleanly to the anatomical metaphor of 'belly,' both implying being swallowed into a confining interior space.
The nearly unanimous historical consensus equates the sign exclusively with Christ's death and burial, pointing to the tomb as the literal interior of the earth.
book_explanatory_advantages: It grounds the phrase 'heart of the earth' in explicit, prior scriptural definitions (Ezekiel 5:5; 38:12) rather than inventing a one-off metaphor for the grave.
It mathematically resolves the 'three days and three nights' without forcing partial days or irregular chronologies.
It completes a massive, scene-by-scene alignment of the Jonah narrative (the ship, the sleep, the storm, the lots, the questioning, the surrender) with the Passion narrative.
It maintains consistent symbolic scale by contrasting the 'heart of the seas' (center of the gentile nations) with the 'heart of the earth' (center of the covenant land).
counter_explanatory_advantages: It focuses purely on the burial and resurrection as the paramount 'sign,' mapping directly to 1 Corinthians 15:3-4 without needing to include the betrayal and trial as part of the core timeline.
It allows for a simple surface-level visual parallel: a body buried in the dirt vs. a body swallowed by a fish.
unresolved_objections: Translating 'earth' (Greek: gē) locally as 'land' (referring to Israel) is valid but relies on a contextual reading rather than a strict global definition of the earth.

Shifting the starting point of the Sign of Jonah to the night of the arrest displaces the exclusive focus on the crucifixion/entombment that many traditionalists view as functionally required by Christian orthodoxy.
